rules.why_matters: SSRF can lead to: - Reading internal services (metadata APIs, databases, internal APIs) - Port scanning your internal network - Exfiltrating sensitive data - Bypassing network-level access controls
what_it_checks: `file_get_contents()`, `curl_init()`, `curl_exec()`, `fopen()`, and `fsockopen()` with tainted URLs
HTTP client libraries (Guzzle, Symfony HttpClient) with user-controlled URLs

rules.title: E0104: HTTP Response Splitting
rules.plain_english: Writing user input to HTTP headers without sanitizing CRLF sequences (`\r\n`) can allow an attacker to inject additional headers or split the HTTP response.
rules.why_matters: HTTP response splitting can: - Inject malicious headers (for example `Set-Cookie` or `Location`) - Enable cache poisoning - Enable cross-site scripting (XSS) in some contexts - Bypass security controls
what_it_checks: `header()` calls with tainted input that may contain CRLF sequences
`setcookie()` with tainted values that may contain newlines

rules.title: E0105: Local File Inclusion
rules.plain_english: Including or reading a local file based on user-controlled input can allow an attacker to read arbitrary files on your server or execute code.
rules.why_matters: Local file inclusion (LFI) can: - Read sensitive files (`/etc/passwd`, source code, credentials, config files) - Include uploaded files containing malicious PHP code - Lead to remote code execution when combined with file upload
rules.bad_example:
$page = $_GET['page'] ?? '';
include __DIR__ . '/pages/' . $page . '.php';
what_it_checks: `include`, `require`, `include_once`, and `require_once` with paths built from tainted input
`file_get_contents()`, `file()`, `readfile()`, and `fopen()` with tainted paths
`../` or null byte (`%00`) sequences in user-controlled paths

rules.title: E0106: Deserialization of Untrusted Data
rules.plain_english: Deserializing untrusted data using `unserialize()` or `wddx_deserialize()` can instantiate arbitrary PHP objects and trigger magic methods, leading to object injection.
rules.why_matters: Deserialization of untrusted data is a critical vulnerability. Attackers can: - Instantiate arbitrary PHP classes - Trigger magic methods (`__wakeup()`, `__destruct()`) - Execute arbitrary code through gadget chains - Achieve remote code execution
what_it_checks: `unserialize()` calls with tainted input from superglobals
`wddx_deserialize()` calls with any argument (inherently dangerous)
`session_decode()` with user-controlled data

rules.title: E0107: Weak Random for Security Tokens
rules.plain_english: Generating security-sensitive tokens (session tokens, CSRF tokens, password reset tokens, API keys) with weak random number generators like `rand()`, `mt_rand()`, or `uniqid()` can make them predictable.
rules.why_matters: Weak random values are predictable. Attackers can: - Guess session tokens and hijack user sessions - Predict CSRF tokens and bypass CSRF protection - Guess password reset tokens and take over accounts - Recover API keys and access protected resources
rules.bad_example:
$token = bin2hex(mt_rand(100000, 999999)); // predictable
$resetToken = uniqid();                    // guessable
rules.good_example:
$token = bin2hex(random_bytes(16));   // cryptographically secure
$resetToken = random_int(100000, 999999); // cryptographically secure
what_it_checks: `rand()`, `mt_rand()`, or `uniqid()` used for security-sensitive purposes (tokens, keys, salts)
`mt_rand()` or `rand()` assigned to variables named `token`, `key`, `secret`, `salt`, `nonce`, or `csrf`

rules.title: E0108: Dynamic Instantiation
rules.plain_english: Instantiating a class using a name that comes from user input can allow an attacker to instantiate any autoloadable class, potentially leading to object injection.
rules.why_matters: Combined with gadget chains, dynamic class instantiation can: - Instantiate any autoloadable class - Trigger object injection via magic methods - Lead to remote code execution
rules.bad_example:
$class = $_GET['class'] ?? '';
$obj = new $class();
what_it_checks: `new $class()` where `$class` comes from superglobal array access
`ReflectionClass::newInstanceArgs()` with a tainted class name
`class_exists()` followed by instantiation of user-controlled class names

rules.title: E0109: Directory Listing Exposure
rules.plain_english: Using `opendir()`, `readdir()`, `scandir()`, or `glob()` on a user-controlled directory path can allow an attacker to list files in arbitrary directories on your server.
rules.why_matters: Directory listing exposure can: - Reveal file names and directory structure - Expose backup files, configuration files, or source code - Help attackers plan further attacks
what_it_checks: `opendir()`, `readdir()`, `scandir()`, and `glob()` with user-controlled directory paths
Directory traversal patterns (`../`) in directory arguments

rules.title: E0110: Raw SQL Query Execution
rules.plain_english: Executing raw SQL queries without prepared statements or parameter binding can make the application vulnerable to SQL injection.
rules.why_matters: Raw SQL execution with user input can lead to: - Data theft (emails, passwords, credit cards) - Authentication bypass - Data modification or deletion - Full server compromise
rules.bad_example:
$id = $_GET['id'] ?? '';
$result = $pdo->query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $id");
what_it_checks: `PDO::query()`, `mysqli_query()`, and `pg_query()` with SQL strings containing interpolated variables
SQL queries built by string concatenation with user input

rules.title: E0111: Deprecated mysql Extension
rules.plain_english: Using removed `ext/mysql` functions (`mysql_connect()`, `mysql_query()`, etc.) causes fatal errors on PHP 7.0+ and lacks prepared statement support.
rules.why_matters: The original `ext/mysql` extension was removed in PHP 7.0. Any code using these functions will crash with a fatal error on PHP 7.0+. The extension also lacks support for prepared statements, making it inherently vulnerable to SQL injection.
what_it_checks: `mysql_connect()`, `mysql_pconnect()`, `mysql_select_db()`, `mysql_query()`, `mysql_fetch_assoc()`, `mysql_fetch_array()`, `mysql_num_rows()`, `mysql_real_escape_string()`, `mysql_error()`, `mysql_errno()`
Any function with the `mysql_` prefix (except `mysqlnd`, which is a driver, not the extension)

rules.title: E0112: File Upload Without Validation
rules.plain_english: Calling `move_uploaded_file()` without validating the uploaded file's extension, MIME type, or destination can allow an attacker to upload malicious files.
rules.why_matters: Unrestricted file upload can lead to: - Remote code execution via uploaded PHP scripts - Server compromise - Distribution of malware through your server
rules.bad_example: move_uploaded_file($_FILES['file']['tmp_name'], '/uploads/' . $_FILES['file']['name']);
what_it_checks: `move_uploaded_file()` without prior extension/MIME validation
`file_put_contents()` with `$_FILES` data
`$_FILES['name']` used directly in file paths

rules.title: E0113: Session Regeneration Missing
rules.plain_english: Calling `session_start()` and writing session data after authentication without calling `session_regenerate_id()` can leave the application vulnerable to session fixation attacks.
rules.why_matters: Session fixation allows an attacker to: - Authenticate using a session ID they chose - Hijack the session after the victim logs in - Access the victim's authenticated account
what_it_checks: `session_start()` followed by `$_SESSION` writes without a subsequent `session_regenerate_id()`
Login/auth endpoints that set session data without regenerating the ID

rules.title: E0114: PHP Info Disclosure
rules.plain_english: Calling `phpinfo()` in committed production code exposes detailed PHP configuration, version, extensions, and environment variables to anyone who can access the page.
rules.why_matters: Attackers can use `phpinfo()` output to: - Fingerprint the server (PHP version, loaded extensions) - Find version-specific vulnerabilities - Read environment variables and configuration values - Plan targeted attacks against your infrastructure
rules.bad_example: <?php phpinfo(); ?>
rules.good_example:
// Remove phpinfo() entirely from production code
// Use it only in local development, never commit it
what_it_checks: `phpinfo()` function calls anywhere in committed source code
`phpinfo(INFO_ALL)`, `phpinfo(INFO_GENERAL)`, and similar calls

rules.title: E0115: XXE via libxml
rules.plain_english: Parsing XML from untrusted input with libxml functions can allow XML External Entity (XXE) attacks when external entities are resolved.
rules.why_matters: XXE vulnerabilities can: - Expose local files such as `/etc/passwd`, source code, or credentials - Trigger server-side request forgery (SSRF) against internal services - Cause denial of service through entity expansion
what_it_checks: `simplexml_load_string()`, `DOMDocument::loadXML()`, `DOMDocument::load()` with tainted input and `LIBXML_NOENT`, or without `LIBXML_NONET`
`xml_parser_create()` / `xml_parse()` with default entity handling

rules.title: E0116: Remote command execution via popen
rules.plain_english: Passing untrusted input to `popen()` can allow an attacker to execute arbitrary shell commands on the server.
rules.why_matters: Command injection through `popen()` can: - Run arbitrary system commands - Read or modify files and databases - Install malware or backdoors - Lead to full server compromise
what_it_checks: `popen()` calls where the command string contains tainted input from superglobals
`popen()` calls with user-controlled command arguments without `escapeshellcmd()` or `escapeshellarg()`

rules.title: E0117: SQL injection via query string
rules.plain_english: Building SQL queries by concatenating query string input (`$_GET`) can allow SQL injection.
rules.why_matters: SQL injection through query string parameters is risky because: - Query parameters are easy to modify and share in URLs - Attacks can be automated with simple URL manipulation - Search and filter endpoints are common targets
rules.bad_example:
$id = $_GET['id'] ?? '';
$result = mysqli_query($conn, "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $id");
what_it_checks: `mysqli_query()`, `PDO::query()`, `pg_query()` with SQL strings containing `$_GET` variables
SQL queries built by string concatenation with query string input

rules.title: E0118: Log forging via user input
rules.plain_english: Writing unsanitized user input to logs can allow log forging, where an attacker injects fake log entries or corrupts log structure.
rules.why_matters: Log forging can: - Hide malicious activity by injecting misleading log entries - Create false audit trail records - Corrupt log files and make incident response harder - Mislead anyone investigating system behavior
rules.bad_example:
error_log("User {$_GET['username']} logged in");
// ?username=admin%0d%0aInjection: fake admin login
rules.good_example:
$username = str_replace(["\r", "\n"], '', $_GET['username'] ?? '');
error_log("User $username logged in");
what_it_checks: `error_log()`, `syslog()`, `trigger_error()` with tainted superglobals directly interpolated
Custom log writers such as `file_put_contents($log, $user_input)` with user input

rules.title: E0119: Session cookie without Secure flag
rules.plain_english: Session cookies configured without the `Secure` flag can be sent over unencrypted HTTP connections, increasing the risk of interception.
rules.why_matters: Without the `Secure` flag on session cookies: - Session IDs can be exposed through network sniffing - Attackers on the same network may be able to hijack sessions - Authentication is more vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks
what_it_checks: `session_set_cookie_params()` with `secure => false`, or where `secure` is not set
`ini_set('session.cookie_secure', '0')`, or cases where it is not set
Session cookies created without the `Secure` attribute

rules.title: E0120: Eval with user-controlled string
rules.plain_english: Calling `eval()` with a string that includes user-controlled input allows arbitrary PHP code execution.
rules.why_matters: `eval()` with user input is a critical security risk: - An attacker can execute arbitrary system commands - It can lead to full server compromise - Data on the server may be read, modified, or deleted
rules.bad_example:
$code = $_GET['code'] ?? '';
eval("return $code;");
what_it_checks: `eval()` calls where the string argument contains tainted input
String concatenation inside `eval()` with user-controlled variables

rules.title: E0121: Assert with user-controlled string
rules.plain_english: Calling `assert()` with a string argument that contains user-controlled input can lead to code execution. In older PHP versions, string arguments to `assert()` are evaluated as PHP code.
rules.why_matters: `assert()` with a string argument can act as a code execution sink: - An attacker may be able to execute arbitrary PHP code - It can lead to full server compromise - String arguments to `assert()` were deprecated in PHP 7.2 and removed in PHP 8.0
what_it_checks: `assert()` calls where the argument is a string containing tainted input
String concatenation inside `assert()` with user-controlled variables

rules.title: E0122: File inclusion with user input
rules.plain_english: Using `include` or `require` with a path built from user-controlled input can allow an attacker to include unintended local or remote files.
rules.why_matters: File inclusion vulnerabilities can: - Include and execute malicious PHP files (local or remote) - Expose sensitive files such as `/etc/passwd`, source code, or configuration files - Lead to remote code execution in some configurations
what_it_checks: `include`, `require`, `include_once`, `require_once` with paths containing tainted input
`$_GET`, `$_POST`, `$_REQUEST`, `$_COOKIE` values used directly in include paths

rules.title: E0123: XSS via echo
rules.plain_english: Outputting user-controlled input directly with `echo`, `print`, or similar constructs without escaping can allow cross-site scripting (XSS).
rules.why_matters: XSS vulnerabilities can: - Steal session cookies and authentication tokens - Perform actions on behalf of another user - Alter page content - Redirect users to malicious sites
rules.good_example:
$name = $_GET['name'] ?? '';
echo "Hello, " . htmlspecialchars($name, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8');
what_it_checks: `echo`, `print`, `printf()`, `vprintf()` with tainted input
`<?= $var ?>` short echo tags with unescaped variables

rules.title: E0124: Weak hash for passwords
rules.plain_english: Hashing passwords with weak algorithms such as MD5, SHA1, or `crypt()` does not provide adequate protection for password storage. Use a dedicated password hashing function instead.
rules.why_matters: Weak password hashing makes it easier for attackers to: - Crack password hashes quickly using rainbow tables or brute-force attacks - Recover common passwords in a short time - Compromise many accounts if a password database is exposed
rules.bad_example:
$hash = md5($password);       // weak, fast, unsalted
$hash = sha1($password);      // weak, fast, unsalted
$hash = crypt($password);     // weak, may use DES-based crypt
what_it_checks: `md5()`, `sha1()`, `hash('md5', ...)`, `hash('sha1', ...)` applied to password-like variables
`crypt()` used for password hashing

rules.title: E0125: Open redirect via header
rules.plain_english: Redirecting users with `header("Location: ...")` to a URL taken from user input without validation can create an open redirect vulnerability.
rules.why_matters: Open redirects can be abused for: - Phishing, by making malicious links appear to come from a trusted domain - Bypassing expectations around post-login redirects - Redirecting users to sites that attempt to steal credentials or deliver malicious content
what_it_checks: `header("Location: ...")` with tainted input
`header("refresh: ...;url=...")` with tainted input

rules.title: E0126: Path traversal via file_get_contents
rules.plain_english: Reading files with `file_get_contents()` (or similar functions) using a path built from user input can allow path traversal if `../` sequences or other unsafe path components are not properly restricted.
rules.why_matters: Path traversal vulnerabilities can: - Expose sensitive files such as `/etc/passwd`, source code, credentials, or configuration files - Reveal environment details and application secrets - Help attackers gather information for further attacks
what_it_checks: `file_get_contents()`, `file()`, `readfile()`, `fopen()` with paths built from tainted input
User-controlled paths that may include `../` or null byte (`%00`) sequences

rules.title: E0127: Command execution via system
rules.plain_english: Passing untrusted input to `system()` can allow an attacker to execute arbitrary shell commands on the server.
rules.why_matters: Command injection through `system()` can: - Run arbitrary system commands - Read or modify files and databases - Install malware or backdoors - Lead to full server compromise
rules.bad_example:
$ip = $_GET['ip'] ?? '';
system("ping -c 4 $ip");
what_it_checks: `system()`, `exec()`, `shell_exec()`, `passthru()` calls with tainted input
Backtick operator (`` `$cmd` ``) with tainted input (also covered by E0087)

rules.title: E0128: Command execution via exec
rules.plain_english: Passing untrusted input to `exec()` can allow an attacker to execute arbitrary shell commands on the server.
rules.why_matters: Command injection through `exec()` can: - Run arbitrary system commands - Read or modify files and databases - Install malware or backdoors - Lead to full server compromise
rules.bad_example:
$cmd = $_GET['cmd'] ?? '';
exec($cmd, $output);
what_it_checks: `exec()` calls where the command string contains tainted input
`exec()` calls with user-controlled command arguments without escaping

rules.title: E0129: Command execution via shell_exec
rules.plain_english: Passing untrusted input to `shell_exec()` can allow an attacker to execute arbitrary shell commands on the server.
rules.why_matters: Command injection through `shell_exec()` can: - Run arbitrary system commands - Read or modify files and databases - Install malware or backdoors - Lead to full server compromise
what_it_checks: `shell_exec()` calls where the command string contains tainted input
`shell_exec()` calls with user-controlled command arguments without escaping

rules.title: E0130: Command execution via passthru
rules.plain_english: Passing untrusted input to `passthru()` can allow an attacker to execute arbitrary shell commands on the server.
rules.why_matters: Command injection through `passthru()` can: - Run arbitrary system commands - Read or modify files and databases - Install malware or backdoors - Lead to full server compromise
rules.bad_example:
$cmd = $_GET['cmd'] ?? '';
passthru($cmd);
what_it_checks: `passthru()` calls where the command string contains tainted input
`passthru()` calls with user-controlled command arguments without escaping

rules.title: E0131: Command execution via proc_open
rules.plain_english: Passing untrusted input to `proc_open()` as part of a command can allow an attacker to execute arbitrary shell commands on the server.
rules.why_matters: Command injection through `proc_open()` can: - Run arbitrary system commands - Read or modify files and databases - Install malware or backdoors - Lead to full server compromise
what_it_checks: `proc_open()` calls where the command string contains tainted input
`proc_open()` calls with user-controlled command arguments without `escapeshellarg()` or `escapeshellcmd()`

rules.title: E0132: Header injection via header
rules.plain_english: Writing user-controlled input to HTTP headers with `header()` without sanitizing CRLF sequences (`\r\n`) can allow HTTP header injection.
rules.why_matters: Header injection can: - Inject malicious headers such as `Set-Cookie`, `Location`, or `Content-Type` - Enable cache poisoning - Contribute to cross-site scripting (XSS) in some contexts - Bypass security controls that rely on header values
what_it_checks: `header()` calls with tainted input that may contain CRLF sequences
`header()` calls where user input is interpolated into the header value

rules.title: E0133: Header injection via setcookie
rules.plain_english: Writing user-controlled input to cookie names or values with `setcookie()` or `setrawcookie()` without sanitizing CRLF sequences can allow HTTP header injection.
rules.why_matters: Header injection through cookie APIs can: - Inject additional `Set-Cookie` headers with attacker-controlled values - Inject other HTTP headers such as `Location` or `Content-Type` - Contribute to session fixation or cookie manipulation attacks
what_it_checks: `setcookie()` or `setrawcookie()` calls where the cookie name or value contains tainted input
Cookie names or values that may contain CRLF sequences

rules.title: E0134: Mail injection via mail
rules.plain_english: Passing unsanitized user input to `mail()` header or subject parameters can allow email header injection.
rules.why_matters: Mail injection can: - Turn a contact form into a spam relay - Send emails to unintended recipients with forged headers - Bypass email filtering and security controls - Harm the sending domain's email reputation
what_it_checks: `mail()` calls where user input is passed to the `$additional_headers` parameter
`mail()` calls where user input is passed to the `$subject` parameter
CRLF sequences (`\r\n`) in mail headers or subject

rules.title: E0135: PHP info disclosure
rules.plain_english: Calling `phpinfo()` in committed code exposes detailed PHP configuration and environment information.
rules.why_matters: `phpinfo()` output can reveal: - PHP version, loaded extensions, and server configuration - Environment variables and configuration values - Information that helps attackers identify version-specific weaknesses and plan targeted attacks
rules.bad_example: <?php phpinfo(); ?>
rules.good_example:
// Remove phpinfo() entirely from production code.
// Use it only in local development and do not commit it.
what_it_checks: `phpinfo()` function calls anywhere in committed source code
`phpinfo(INFO_ALL)`, `phpinfo(INFO_GENERAL)`, and other `phpinfo(...)` variants
